item_name: RADIO COMMUNICATION, AIRMANSHIP, EMERGENCY PROCEDURES, GENERAL KNOWLEDGE.

error_modes.label: Radio Comm. - standard R/T procedures and phraseology on initial contact

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology that left the intention ambiguous to the controller, did not obtain contact with the ground station following the standard procedures and phraseology. Three consecutive clearance read-backs were incorrect or omitted, and SP transmitted over an ongoing exchange between the controller and another A/C. IP had to take the radios and re-establish the approach clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology on the initial contact after each frequency change, did not use the standard format for callsign, level and intentions. Two read-backs were incomplete and were corrected only after the IP prompted on interphone, and one initial contact was made while the controller was still transmitting. R/T procedure remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed initial call after the frequency change, transmitted callsign and level in non-standard order. SP recognized the error without any prompt, re-transmitted correctly within the same exchange and used standard phraseology for the remainder of the sortie. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP established two-way communication with every station using the standard format and phraseology. Initial contact after each frequency change was made without interrupting ongoing traffic, and all clearances were read back completely and accurately on the first transmission.
texts.4: SP transmitted with complete standard phraseology throughout, including the approach clearance, the holding instruction and the missed approach. Calls were concise, correctly sequenced and consistently made in the first available gap in traffic. No transmission required repetition by the controller.
texts.marginal: SP used standard phraseology and read back all clearances correctly, but transmissions were consistently long and obliged the controller to wait for a gap. Every call was within the standard, yet the pattern trended toward occupying the frequency during the busiest phase of the approach. SP is expected to shorten the standard calls so that correct phraseology is delivered at a normal transmission rate.

error_modes.label: Radio Comm. - continuous radio watch and response timeliness

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted radio watch while re-tuning the navigation aid, did not continuously monitor radio communication. Four calls addressed to the aircraft went unanswered and the controller repeated the descent clearance twice. IP answered on behalf of the crew to prevent a loss of separation.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the approach plate, responded late to calls from the ground station. Three calls required a second transmission by the controller before SP replied, and the reply was made only after the IP prompted on interphone. Radio watch remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a cockpit task carried into the descent, missed one call from the ground station. SP recognized the missed call from the traffic on frequency, requested the transmission again on his own initiative and answered all subsequent calls without delay. No IP prompt was required.
texts.3: SP continuously monitored the frequency and answered every call addressed to the aircraft on the first transmission. Radio watch was maintained through the approach and through all frequency changes without a single call being missed.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted radio watch for the whole mission, answering every call immediately while continuing to fly the procedure accurately. SP also retained calls addressed to other aircraft that affected the sequence and used them to anticipate the controller's instructions.
texts.marginal: SP answered all calls within the required time, but responses during the highest workload segment of the approach were consistently at the slowest end of the acceptable range. No delay ever required a second transmission by the controller, yet the trend showed the radio watch competing with the instrument cross-check. SP is expected to hold the response time constant regardless of the workload phase.

error_modes.label: Radio Comm. - accurate compliance with ATC instructions

texts.0: SP, due to a clearance misinterpreted and never verified with the controller, did not precisely follow the instructions given by the ground station. SP descended to a level that had not been cleared and turned opposite to the assigned heading. IP intervened to stop the descent and to obtain a corrected clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to a clearance copied incompletely and not verified with the controller, entered the holding pattern on the wrong inbound course. The error was corrected only after two verbal directions from the IP, and the correction was applied late in the turn. Compliance remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a partially copied clearance, initially set an incorrect assigned heading. SP detected the discrepancy against his own written copy, requested confirmation from the controller and complied with the correct heading before the deviation became significant. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP followed every instruction from the ground station precisely and without misinterpretation. Headings, levels and speed assignments were read back correctly and complied with promptly on each occasion.
texts.4: SP complied with every instruction exactly and immediately, including two amended clearances issued during the approach. SP verified each non-standard instruction with the controller before executing it, and no assigned parameter was ever flown incorrectly.
texts.marginal: SP complied correctly with all instructions, but on the amended clearances SP needed the full read-back to reconstruct what had been assigned before acting. Compliance stayed within standards, yet the trend showed dependence on the read-back rather than on an accurate first copy. SP is expected to copy clearances accurately at first transmission so that compliance is immediate.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - orientation and instrument cross-check against A/C position

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the navigation display, did not continuously monitor the control and performance instruments or crosscheck them with the A/C position. SP lost orientation in the holding pattern and allowed the aircraft to leave both the protected area and the assigned level. IP took control to re-establish the aircraft on the published pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of the primary flight instruments across the configuration changes, did not crosscheck aircraft performance against position. Heading and level deviations developed on three occasions and were corrected only after verbal directions from the IP, each after a noticeable delay. The cross-check remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a temporary fixation on the approach chart, allowed the cross-check to slow during the descent. SP recognized the developing deviation on the control and performance instruments, restored the scan on his own initiative and corrected the aircraft state before it became significant. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP continuously monitored the control and performance instruments and crosschecked them with the aircraft position throughout the mission. Orientation was maintained at all times and the required corrections were applied promptly and in the correct priority.
texts.4: SP maintained an unbroken and correctly prioritized cross-check for the whole sortie, including through configuration changes and amended clearances. Orientation with respect to the procedure was never in doubt, and corrections were anticipated rather than reactive.
texts.marginal: SP maintained orientation and a correct cross-check, but the scan slowed each time a new radio task arrived and corrections were applied at the late end of the acceptable range. Performance stayed within standards, yet the trend indicated that the cross-check was being displaced by secondary tasks. SP is expected to hold the cross-check rate constant while working the radios.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - task prioritization and saturation management

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the approach phase, did not put the required tasks in order and became saturated. SP omitted the approach checks and the required position report while attempting to reprogram the navigation aid, and channelized attention on the equipment left the aircraft state unmonitored. IP took control and completed the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated the cockpit workload inside the turn, did not handle the tasks in sequence and dropped two of them. The checks and the level-off were completed only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, each later than required. Task management remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to an unexpected re-clearance, initially attempted to fly, copy and reconfigure at the same time. SP recognized the developing saturation, deferred the non-essential cockpit task and completed the remaining items in the correct order on his own initiative. No task was dropped and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP prioritized the cockpit tasks correctly, without omitting anything significant and without violating any rule. SP handled multiple tasks in sequence throughout the mission and never approached a channelized attention situation.
texts.4: SP maintained a correct task order throughout, including through two amended clearances and one simulated system abnormal. SP shed secondary tasks before saturation could develop and completed every required item at or before the point where it was needed.
texts.marginal: SP kept all tasks in the correct order and dropped nothing, but the margin before saturation was visibly small during the final segment of the approach. Performance remained within standards, yet the trend showed that one additional task would have displaced a required item. SP is expected to sequence cockpit work earlier so that reserve capacity is retained on the approach.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - risk management, decision making and RTB or divert judgment

texts.0: SP, due to continuation of the plan after the weather information that invalidated it had already been received, did not identify the contingencies or the available alternatives. SP did not adjust the execution of the mission to the available flight time and remaining fuel and continued toward an airfield below minima. IP took the decision and directed the diversion.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete gathering of the available data before deciding, did not state the intended course of action clearly and could not provide the rationale for it. The alternate was selected only after two verbal directions from the IP, and the decision was taken later than the fuel state permitted. Decision making remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial assessment that did not account for the actual holding fuel, first elected to continue for a second approach. SP re-evaluated the fuel and weather data without prompting, stated the revised decision clearly with its rationale and diverted with an adequate margin. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP accurately identified the contingencies and the available alternatives, gathered the relevant data and stated each decision clearly with its rationale. SP adjusted the execution of the mission to the available flight time and the remaining fuel, and the potential hazards were recognized and positively avoided.
texts.4: SP identified every contingency in advance, including the deteriorating destination weather, and stated the decision points before they were reached. Each decision was clearly expressed, supported by the actual data and taken early enough that all alternatives remained available.
texts.marginal: SP identified the contingencies and reached correct decisions, but each decision was taken at the last point at which it remained valid. The choices were within standards, yet the trend showed reliance on the final decision point rather than on early assessment. SP is expected to reach the same decisions earlier, while the alternatives are still unconstrained.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - flight discipline, operational checks and SOP compliance

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted check sequence that was never resumed at the correct point, did not perform the operational checks according to the Check List, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. Two required check sequences were omitted and one was performed out of order, and SP did not carry out the duties without supervision. IP had to direct and then verify the aircraft configuration.
texts.1: SP, due to check items deferred until the workload of the approach had already increased, did not carry out all the required steps of the procedures in the proper order. Three check items were completed only after being called by the IP, and the rules applicable to the approach were applied late. Flight discipline remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption caused by a frequency change, started the approach checks out of the published order. SP recognized the deviation, returned to the correct point in the sequence and completed all items without omission before commencing the descent. No IP prompt was required.
texts.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the Check List, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. SP demonstrated knowledge of the applicable rules and regulations and carried out all duties with minimum IP supervision.
texts.4: SP executed every check and procedure in the published sequence and at the correct point, with complete knowledge of the applicable rules and regulations. SP required no supervision at any stage and absorbed two interruptions without a single item being displaced.
texts.marginal: SP completed all checks in the correct order, but consistently started them at the latest acceptable point in the profile. Compliance remained within standards, yet the trend left no margin for an interruption before an item would be missed. SP is expected to initiate the published sequences earlier in each phase.

error_modes.label: Emergency Procedures - BOLD FACE critical action recall and sequence

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient study of the critical action procedures, did not state the BOLD FACE steps by heart or in sequence. SP reversed two steps of the simulated emergency and omitted a third, and the sequence as stated would have aggravated the condition. IP stopped the SP and performed the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete memorization of the critical action steps, stated the BOLD FACE with one step out of sequence and one omission. The sequence was corrected only after the IP prompted the missing item, and the recall was slower than the procedure requires. Knowledge remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a hesitation at the transition between the memory items and the printed checklist, initially stated one BOLD FACE step out of order. SP recognized the error immediately, restated the full sequence correctly without prompting and continued from the correct point. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP stated the proper steps of the critical action procedures in sequence, by heart and without mistakes. Recall was immediate for each simulated emergency presented during the mission.
texts.4: SP stated every BOLD FACE sequence immediately, verbatim and in the correct order, including the procedures presented without warning during the approach. Recall was accurate under workload and did not degrade the aircraft control being flown at the time.
texts.marginal: SP stated all BOLD FACE steps correctly and in sequence, but recall was noticeably slower for the procedures presented in the descent than for those asked during the brief. Knowledge was within standards, yet the trend indicated that the memory items were not fully automatic under workload. SP is expected to reach the same accuracy at a uniform recall speed.

error_modes.label: Emergency Procedures - Check List and IFG execution and effective handling

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on a single caution indication at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not execute the procedures according to the Check List and the IFG. SP worked the malfunction while the aircraft descended below the assigned level, omitted two checklist items and did not handle the emergency effectively. IP took control and completed the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the malfunctioning system, did not execute the checklist steps in the standardized sequence or within the required time. Two items were completed only after verbal direction from the IP, and the aircraft was flown with reduced priority throughout the handling. Execution remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a delay in moving from the memory items to the printed procedure, started the checklist late. SP recognized the delay, resumed the correct sequence without prompting and completed all steps flawlessly while holding the assigned level and heading. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP executed all procedures according to the Check List and the IFG without IP intervention, flawlessly, timely and in the standardized sequence. SP handled each simulated emergency effectively while continuing to fly the aircraft accurately.
texts.4: SP handled every simulated emergency effectively and completed the printed procedures in the standardized sequence without delay or error. Aircraft control and the instrument procedure were maintained at full accuracy throughout the handling, and SP kept the controller informed at each stage.
texts.marginal: SP executed the procedures in the correct sequence and without error, but the transition from the memory items to the printed checklist was consistently slow. Handling stayed within standards, yet the trend showed the printed procedure competing with aircraft control rather than following it smoothly. SP is expected to achieve the same accuracy with a shorter transition.

error_modes.label: Emergency Procedures - knowledge of A/C limits and relevant systems

texts.0: SP, due to no preparation of the daily assignment on the aircraft systems, did not know or observe the A/C limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual. SP quoted three limits incorrectly and could not describe the system affected by the simulated malfunction. IP had to state the limits and explain the system before the procedure could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of Section V of the Flight Manual, quoted two A/C limits incorrectly and required prompting on the operation of the affected system. The correct values were given only after the IP supplied the reference, and the description of the emergency system remained incomplete. Knowledge remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a confusion between two similar limiting values, initially quoted one A/C limit incorrectly. SP recognized the error without prompting, corrected the value and then described the affected system and the associated procedure in detail. No IP correction was required.
texts.3: SP knew and observed the A/C limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual. SP described in detail the emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as daily assignment, answering each question accurately.
texts.4: SP quoted every applicable limit accurately and explained the relevant systems in detail, including the reasons behind each procedural step. SP related the limits to the conditions actually being flown and observed them precisely throughout the mission.
texts.marginal: SP quoted the A/C limits correctly and described the relevant systems, but the answers on the less frequently used systems required time to assemble. Knowledge was within standards, yet the trend showed uneven depth across the assigned material. SP is expected to reach a uniform level of detail across all the systems set as daily assignment.

error_modes.label: General Knowledge - daily assignment and use of flight publications

texts.0: SP, due to no preparation of the material set as daily assignment, did not know the assigned exercises and could not use the Flight Manual, the Techniques and Procedures Manual, the AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 or the aeronautical publications. SP was unable to locate the applicable approach information in the publications. IP had to supply the required data before the mission could proceed.
texts.1: SP, due to superficial preparation of the assigned material, answered fewer than half of the questions on the daily assignment correctly. The relevant references were located only after the IP indicated the publication and the section, and the answers remained incomplete. Knowledge remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a confusion between two similar published procedures, initially gave an incorrect answer on the assigned material. SP recognized the error, located the correct reference in the publication without assistance and completed the answer. No IP correction was required.
texts.3: SP knew in detail the exercises given as daily assignment and used the Flight Manual, the Techniques and Procedures Manual, the AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the aeronautical publications with confidence. Every reference required during the briefings was located and applied correctly.
texts.4: SP answered every question on the assigned material accurately and without hesitation, and supported the answers with the exact references from the publications. SP also related the published material to the specific conditions planned for the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP knew the assigned material and located the required references, but the search through the publications was slow on the items not covered in the previous briefing. Knowledge was within standards, yet the trend showed familiarity concentrated on recently used sections. SP is expected to maintain the same fluency across the whole assigned publication set.

error_modes.label: General Knowledge - meteorology, aerodynamics and flight planning

texts.0: SP, due to no study of the meteorological and aerodynamic material, could not follow the morning meteorological briefing or explain the conditions to be encountered during the flight. SP was unable to plan the flight or to state the airport traffic procedures for the destination. IP had to complete the planning.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete knowledge of the meteorological principles, could not interpret the forecast presented at the briefing without assistance. The theoretical explanation of the situations to be encountered was produced only after repeated prompting from the IP, and the flight plan required correction on two items. Knowledge remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to an incorrect reading of one element of the forecast, initially planned the approach for the wrong runway. SP identified the error while reviewing the airport traffic procedures, corrected the plan without prompting and explained the associated aerodynamic considerations correctly. No IP correction was required.
texts.3: SP demonstrated the meteorological knowledge required to attend the morning briefing without difficulty and explained theoretically the situations to be encountered during the flight. SP knew the airport traffic procedures and planned the flight accurately.
texts.4: SP interpreted the meteorological briefing in full, including the implications of the forecast for the planned approach, and explained the relevant aerodynamics precisely. The flight plan was complete, accurate and built around the actual conditions and the applicable traffic procedures.
texts.marginal: SP interpreted the forecast and planned the flight correctly, but the aerodynamic explanation of the conditions to be encountered was given only in general terms. Knowledge was within standards, yet the trend showed application running ahead of the underlying theory. SP is expected to support the same planning decisions with a precise theoretical explanation.

error_modes.label: General Knowledge - flight physiology, survival and SAR rescue procedures

texts.0: SP, due to no preparation of the air medicine and survival material, could not interpret the physiological conditions and flight effects to be encountered and was unaware of the sea and land survival procedures. SP could not state the rescue procedures from SAR means. IP had to brief the entire subject before the mission.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of flight physiology, interpreted two of the physiological effects incorrectly and described the survival procedures only in outline. The correct content was produced only after the IP supplied the key points, and the SAR rescue procedures were stated incompletely. Knowledge remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a confusion between two physiological effects with similar symptoms, initially gave an incorrect interpretation. SP recognized the error, corrected the interpretation without prompting and then described the sea and land survival procedures and the SAR rescue procedures accurately. No IP correction was required.
texts.3: SP demonstrated knowledge of air medicine and flight physiology and interpreted correctly the physiological conditions and flight effects to be encountered. SP was aware of both sea and land survival procedures and of the rescue procedures from SAR means.
texts.4: SP interpreted every physiological condition and flight effect accurately and related them to the profile to be flown. SP described the sea and land survival procedures and the SAR rescue procedures in full detail, including the actions required in each phase.
texts.marginal: SP interpreted the physiological effects correctly and knew the survival procedures, but the answers on the SAR rescue sequence had to be assembled step by step. Knowledge was within standards, yet the trend showed the survival material less consolidated than the physiology. SP is expected to reach the same immediacy across both subjects.

error_modes.label: Radio Comm. - brevity, frequency clutter and controller attention before a detailed request

texts.0: SP, due to added verbiage that is not required on every check-in, cluttered a congested frequency with meaningless phrases instead of providing the controller with the information needed in the format expected. Four transmissions omitted needed information and the controller had to query for the missing part each time, while a long detailed holding request was passed without first getting the controller's attention. The resulting congestion delayed the approach clearance and IP took the radios to restore the flow.
texts.1: SP, due to unnecessary verbiage on the initial call to each new agency, added airtime without adding information on a busy frequency. Two calls omitted information the controller then had to query, and one detailed request was transmitted without first getting the controller's attention. The calls were shortened only after two prompts from the IP on interphone, leaving brevity at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a long detailed request passed without first getting the controller's attention, caused one repetition on a busy frequency. SP recognized the pattern without any prompt, reverted to a short attention call followed by the request after acknowledgement, and kept the remaining transmissions to the information needed in the format expected. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP provided the controller with the information needed, nothing more and nothing less, in the format expected. Detailed requests were preceded by a short attention call and stated only after acknowledgement, and no transmission had to be queried by the controller or repeated by SP.
texts.4: SP kept every transmission brief and complete, with no filler phrases on any frequency change. The detailed requests for holding and for the second approach were split into an attention call and the request itself, keeping airtime to a minimum on a congested frequency. The controller never queried for missing information and no call had to be repeated.
texts.marginal: SP kept the calls within the standard format, but two check-ins carried filler phrases that added airtime without adding information. Brevity was within standards, yet the trend showed the filler increasing as the frequency became busier. SP is expected to strip the non-required verbiage before the workload of the approach phase builds up.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - clearing responsibility under radar monitoring and visual scan technique

texts.0: SP, relying on radar monitoring and ATC separation as if they relieved the pilot of the responsibility to clear, did not search outside during the vectored segments. The eyes stayed inside for the whole descent with no refocus on a distant point after the instrument crosscheck, and two traffic calls passed by approach control were missed. IP took control to ensure the intended flight path stayed well clear of the converging A/C.
texts.1: SP, treating radar monitoring as sufficient separation, searched outside only after the IP prompted at each traffic call. Sectors were swept broadly instead of in arcs of about 20-30 degrees held for 3-5 seconds, and after each instrument crosscheck the eyes remained focused close to the panel. Clearing was maintained at the limit of the standard, with three verbal prompts required during the sortie.
texts.2: SP, due to channelizing on the radio position information, delayed the visual search for the traffic reported at 2 o'clock. SP recognized the omission without any prompt, resumed searching in arcs of about 20-30 degrees with a 3-5 second focus on a distant point, and acquired the A/C well before it closed. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP cleared with both eyes and radios throughout, searching in arcs of about 20-30 degrees and refocusing on a distant point after each instrument crosscheck. The mandatory transmissions at the pattern choke points were made on time and the traffic reported by ATC was acquired visually before any conflict developed.
texts.4: SP treated ATC separation as assistance and never as a substitute for clearing, keeping a disciplined scan in every phase including the vectored and the missed approach segments. Reported traffic was acquired visually on each occasion, a slight heading change was used to create the relative movement needed on one contact that appeared stationary in the canopy, and the intended flight path was kept well clear by more than 500 feet.
texts.marginal: SP cleared adequately and made the mandatory calls at the choke points, but the outside scan thinned each time the instrument workload increased. Clearing remained within standards, yet the trend showed a growing reliance on ATC traffic calls to trigger the search. SP is expected to refocus on a distant point after the crosscheck without waiting for a radio cue.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - checklist discipline, interruptions and (BOTH) challenge and response

texts.0: SP, after being interrupted mid-checklist by a frequency change, resumed at the step where the interruption occurred instead of restarting the checklist or backing up two to three steps. Two items were left uncompleted, a new checklist was started before the previous one was finished, and one (BOTH) item was called complete without any response from the other cockpit. IP stopped the sequence and ran the checklist again from the first step.
texts.1: SP, due to repeated interruptions during the descent, did not positively confirm completion of the checklist and gave lip service to two items by reciting the mnemonic instead of performing the check. The restart came only after the IP pointed out the omission, and one (BOTH) item was treated as complete before the proper response was received. Checklist discipline stayed at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, interrupted by an ATC instruction in the middle of the before landing checklist, initially resumed one step past the interruption. SP caught the break without any prompt, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step and confirmed completion of every remaining item. No item was left uncompleted and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP completed each checklist without starting a new one before the previous was finished, and positively confirmed completion of all of them. Every (BOTH) item was initiated as a challenge and left open until the proper response was received from the other cockpit.
texts.4: SP executed a few items from memory and then referred back to the checklist page to verify completion, so no step was left unconfirmed at any point of the sortie. The two interruptions during the approach checks were absorbed by restarting two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, and every (BOTH) item was closed by challenge and response.
texts.marginal: SP completed all checklists and confirmed them, but the verification of two items was performed from memory alone after the flow had been broken. Checklist discipline was within standards, yet the trend showed the confirmation step being abbreviated as the pace increased. SP is expected to refer back to the page after each interruption rather than rely on recall.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - WHOLDS and let down plate review accomplished in a timely fashion before descent

texts.0: SP, leaving the WHOLDS actions until the descent had already begun, did not review the let down plate and did not recheck destination weather before the IAF. The NAVAIDS were still set for the enroute segment, minimums and the missed approach were unknown at the fix, and lost communication instructions were never coordinated although required. IP had to level the A/C off and rebuild the approach setup before the descent could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to a late start of the WHOLDS sequence, reviewed the let down plate only after the IP prompted on interphone. Destination weather was rechecked past the point of beginning the enroute descent, and minimums and the missed approach were read out while the A/C was already inside the initial approach segment. In-flight checks were accomplished at the limit of the standard for timeliness.
texts.2: SP, with the holding coordination arriving late from ATC, delayed the descent check and the plate review by about one minute past the planned point. SP recognized the delay without any prompt, completed weather, clearance, plate review and descent check before the IAF and slowed for the holding pattern in time. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP accomplished the WHOLDS actions prior to descent from cruising altitude, with weather rechecked before the IAF, clearance obtained and the let down plate reviewed. NAVAIDS, minimums, altimeter, initial descent rate and the missed approach were all covered and the A/C was slowed for holding at the planned point.
texts.4: SP ran the WHOLDS sequence unhurried and complete well before the enroute descent, including lost communication instructions and the aerodrome sketch. The plate review left nothing to be looked up later, so every altitude, course and frequency of the approach was already known when needed. Speed was reduced for holding without any prompt from ATC or the IP.
texts.marginal: SP completed the WHOLDS actions before the descent, but the plate review was compressed and the missed approach was read only once at the last moment. Timeliness was within standards, yet the trend showed the review sliding closer to the IAF with each successive approach. SP is expected to start the sequence early enough to keep the same detail on the later approaches.

error_modes.label: Airmanship - 6 T's, CAT and LIDS actions at the holding fix, IAF and FAF

texts.0: SP, omitting the 6 T's at the holding fix, did not start outbound timing, did not twist the outbound course and left the power at the cruise setting. The entry was flown without established timing, the report of established in the holding pattern was never made, and at the IAF the inbound course and the altimeter setting were still those of the enroute segment. IP had to set the course and altimeter and reposition the A/C for the approach.
texts.1: SP, applying the 6 T's out of sequence at the fix, twisted the course after the turn was already established and adjusted power late, so the outbound leg was flown above the 120-150 KIAS holding band. Timing was started only after the IP prompted, and the CAT actions at the IAF were closed with the altimeter set at the last moment before the descent. Fix actions remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, due to a late frequency change, began the 6 T's a few seconds after crossing the holding fix and had to catch up on timing and course. SP self-corrected within the outbound leg, twisted the correct outbound course, set power for a holding speed inside the 120-150 KIAS band and made the established report without any prompt. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP applied the 6 T's at the holding fix and at the IAF in sequence, with timing started, turn flown, power set for holding speed within 120-150 KIAS, course twisted, track maintained and the required reports transmitted. The CAT actions were completed before each turn and the LIDS items were set before commencing final approach.
texts.4: SP ran the 6 T's, CAT and LIDS without hesitation at every fix, so timing, course and speed were established before the A/C reached each one. Before the FAF the 3 A's were covered as well, with the before landing checklist complete, approach speed set and the runway environment reviewed. No item had to be recalled or corrected later in the approach.
texts.marginal: SP covered the 6 T's at each fix, but Talk was consistently left last and twice the report followed the turn by several seconds. Fix actions were within standards, yet the trend showed the sequence being reconstructed over the fix rather than anticipated before it. SP is expected to have the outbound course and the holding power setting pre-selected before crossing the fix.

error_modes.label: Emergency Procedures - CWS panel check before reset and confirmation of indications before action

texts.0: SP, on the master warning illuminating, pushed the light to reset it before looking at the CWS panel and lost the only indication of the simulated malfunction. Indications were not confirmed with the other crewmember, and critical actions were begun for a problem that had not been positively identified. IP had to stop the sequence, re-establish the diagnosis and re-run the procedure from the beginning.
texts.1: SP, reaching for the master warning light before scanning the CWS panel, identified the simulated malfunction only after the IP directed attention to the caption. Indications were not confirmed with the other crewmember and a second caption on the panel was disregarded while diagnosing the problem. Analysis of the situation remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, in the initial startle of the simulated malfunction, moved a hand toward the master warning light before checking the CWS panel. SP stopped the action without any prompt, read the panel first, confirmed the indications with the other crewmember and only then proceeded with the identified procedure. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained A/C control, looked at the CWS panel before resetting the master warning light and confirmed the indications with the other crewmember. All indications were considered before the problem was declared identified and the critical actions followed that positive identification.
texts.4: SP kept attitude, power and trim set for control while reading every caption on the CWS panel and crosschecking the associated engine and system indications. The diagnosis was stated aloud, confirmed with the other crewmember and matched against all available indications before any action was taken. The reset of the master warning light followed the analysis rather than preceding it.
texts.marginal: SP checked the CWS panel before the reset and identified the simulated malfunction correctly, but the confirmation with the other crewmember was reduced to a single word. Analysis was within standards, yet the trend showed the crosscheck being shortened as the workload of the recovery increased. SP is expected to keep the confirmation explicit for the whole sequence.

error_modes.label: Emergency Procedures - post boldface re-check of A/C control and declaring with a plan
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 Tabletop and Stand-up Emergency Procedures (EPs)

texts.0: SP, after executing the critical actions, did not refer back to A/C control and left the A/C to decelerate and yaw when the PCL was moved below 60 %. No check was made to verify that the boldface had achieved what it was intended to do and no further applicable procedure was considered. The call to ATC gave neither time to landing nor a plan of action, and IP had to fly the A/C and pass the emergency call.
texts.1: SP, moving straight from the critical actions to the cleanup checklist, re-checked A/C control only after the IP prompted, by which time the stick, rudder and PCL compensation for the reduced power was overdue. The verification that the procedure had produced its intended effect was not repeated, and the call to ATC omitted souls on board and the plan of action until the controller asked. Handling of the emergency stayed at the limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, focused on the cleanup items, initially skipped the re-check of the engine indications after the boldface. SP caught the omission without any prompt, repeated the FEVER check, confirmed that the procedure had done what it was intended to do and then asked whether another boldface applied. The declaration that followed carried the nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board and the plan of action.
texts.3: SP referred back to A/C control after each critical action and each checklist, compensating with control stick, rudder and PCL for the reduced power. SP verified with a further check that the procedure had done what it was intended to do, established that no other boldface applied and declared to ATC with a complete plan.
texts.4: SP looped through A/C control, analysis and procedure without any prompting, re-checking the indications after every step and establishing that no further critical action applied. The declaration gave the nature of the emergency, time to landing, souls on board and the plan of action, including the pattern to be flown and how the A/C would be stopped. SP had also fixed in advance the altitude at which ejection would be initiated if the situation deteriorated.
texts.marginal: SP re-checked A/C control after the critical actions and declared with a plan, but the ejection decision altitude was stated only after the recovery was already established. Handling was within standards, yet the trend showed the deteriorating case being considered last rather than in advance. SP is expected to fix that decision point while there is still time to use it.

error_modes.label: Emergency Procedures - single engine mentality, ELP glide profile and minimum ejection altitude

texts.0: SP, with no running awareness of the nearest suitable emergency airfields, selected a field whose elevation was left out of the glide distance calculation and pressed a profile that could not be flown. No minimum ejection altitude was set, the intervening terrain along the route was ignored, and SP continued toward the field after the update points had shown the glide profile was already low. IP took control, turned to the closer field and restored the ELP profile.
texts.1: SP, not tracking the nearest suitable airfield during the cruise segment, needed IP prompting to select a recovery field and then omitted field elevation from the glide distance estimate. The minimum ejection altitude was set only after a second prompt and the glide profile was assessed once instead of at each update point. Single engine handling remained at the limit of the standard for this axis.
texts.2: SP, in the first assessment, considered only the distance to the field and left the intervening terrain out of the plan. SP corrected without any prompt, added field elevation and terrain to the glide calculation, selected update points along the profile and set a minimum ejection altitude before the descent developed further. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained awareness of the nearest suitable emergency airfields throughout, and the field selected accounted for elevation, intervening terrain, winds and weather on the recovery route. A minimum ejection altitude was set, the restart decision was argued through fire, FOD and seizure, and the glide profile was assessed at each update point.
texts.4: SP responded to the unusual engine indications conservatively and had the recovery field, the ELP glide profile and the minimum ejection altitude established before the analysis was complete. The restart decision was reasoned through fire, FOD and seizure, and SP stated the point on the profile at which recovery would be abandoned in favor of ejection. Every update point confirmed the A/C was on profile.
texts.marginal: SP kept a suitable field in mind and set a minimum ejection altitude, but the glide profile was assessed at the first update point only and the terrain along the route was raised late. Handling was within standards, yet the trend showed the profile being accepted rather than re-checked as the glide progressed. SP is expected to keep assessing the profile at every update point.
